analysis.one_liner: Equalizes campaign contribution limits, letting individuals give more while capping PAC donations at the same level.
analysis.headline: The bill was never considered by any committee or voted on by the House; it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal campaign contribution limits so that individuals and political action committees (PACs) faced the same ceiling. Individuals could give a candidate up to $3,000 per election instead of $1,000, while multicandidate PACs would be capped at $3,000 instead of their $5,000 limit [S3]. It also delayed any change until elections held more than six years after passage [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Oversight Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy individual donors gain the most: they could give three times as much to each candidate ($3,000 instead of $1,000) [S3]. Campaign finance groups that have long argued PAC money ties candidates to organized interests would also see one of their goals met, since multicandidate PACs would lose their higher $5,000 limit and be held to the same $3,000 ceiling as individuals [S3]. Candidates would spend more time courting large individual donors.

how_it_helps.text: It triples the amount an individual donor can give to a candidate, from $1,000 to $3,000 per election, giving donors with more disposable income greater per-candidate giving power.
It cuts the multicandidate PAC limit from $5,000 to $3,000, reducing the advantage organized interests had over individual donors and making the rules the same for everyone.

analysis.who_pays: Multicandidate PACs — the vehicles through which unions, corporations, and advocacy groups pool member or shareholder money — would lose a third of their per-candidate giving power, dropping from $5,000 to $3,000 per election [S3]. Candidates and parties would also have to adapt to raising money from a different mix of donors. The bill's six-year delay before taking effect [S3] means voters would see no change for several election cycles.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multicandidate PACs, unions and corporate interests

drawbacks.text: Tripling the individual limit to $3,000 mainly benefits donors who can afford to write large checks, increasing the weight of big-dollar money in campaigns rather than reducing it.

The bill's own effective date postponed any change until elections held more than six years after enactment, so even if it had passed in 1995 the new rules would not have applied until elections well into the 2000s.

Cutting the PAC limit without addressing other channels could push organized-interest money toward less-regulated routes, since groups that lose a direct contribution channel historically shift spending to independent expenditures and soft money — a common dynamic when contribution limits are tightened on one channel only.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine attempt to level the rules — one limit for everyone — and the PAC cut addresses a long-standing reform complaint that organized interests outgun individual donors. But the trade it strikes is double-edged: the money freed from PAC limits is replaced by tripling what the wealthiest individuals can give, so the total influence of big money is not reduced, just re-sorted toward rich donors. The six-year delayed effective date further weakened whatever value it had.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Oversight Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Whitfield introduced the bill on June 15, 1995, delivering introductory remarks the same day.
It was referred to the House Committee on House Oversight, which has jurisdiction over election law, and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point.
When the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, the bill died without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multicandidate PACs and the organized interests behind them came out ahead: the existing system, with PACs giving up to $5,000 and individuals capped at $1,000, stayed in place untouched.

for.name: Rep. Ed Whitfield
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on June 15, 1995.

against.name: House Committee on House Oversight
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over federal election law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded support was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Multicandidate political action committees (union, corporate, and ideological PACs)
industries.note: PACs would lose their $5,000 per-candidate limit and drop to $3,000, the same as individuals, shrinking their organized-giving advantage [S3]. Reformers view PAC money as a channel for special-interest access, so the cut arguably serves the public; the PACs themselves would bear the cost.

The individual limit would triple from $1,000 to $3,000 per election, multiplying the giving power of people who can afford large checks [S3]. More big-donor money means candidates are more responsive to the wealthiest contributors, not less.
